I've eaten these (particularly the chicken 🐔 flavor) for years & so did my 3 kids! It's a true life saver, in this terrible economy!! The seasoning is flavorful as is, but you could also, easily add in a few diced green onions, carrots or maybe even a handful of tiny, Bok Choy bits or shredded green cabbage with a sprinkle of ground Ginger), just for a change of pace! For each package (I always cook 2 packages at a time), simply pour 2 cups of water into a 2 quart sauce or pasta pan & then bring water to a slow boil, but add the seasoning mix from the foil packet, into the water and stir with a whisk or fork BEFORE the water boils (so that the seasoning is distributed more evenly & won't clump up). Then? Add the noodles and IMMEDIATELY lower the stove temperature (a 'mediuum to slow' is good, or it will boil over)! Cook for LESS THAN 3 MINUTES (to avoid soggy noodles). Stir frequently while boiling on low heat, in order to avoid noodles sticking to each other & some being "undercooked." If a little too much water inadvertently evaporates while cooking but you want more broth? You can add another 1/2 cup of water, about 2 minutes into boil (helps cool it down faster too) along with a quick dash of salt 🧂, to keep it from tasting "bland," after you added the extra water. Otherwise, just don't add any extra water or salt & eat as is. Then... enjoy! 😋 PERFECT IN COLD WINTER WEATHER... it's right up there with "Mom's grilled cheese 🥪 sandwiches" (& tomato soup 🍲 combos) on a cold day, when we were kids! Then, just enjoy and smile. 😋

I had never heard of Pierce Brown when, months ago, I bought the Kindle version of Red Rising because I wanted something new and the price was right. How has that worked out for me? Extremely well, thank you. Red Rising is a book that is sometimes likened to The Hunger Games, due to its central plot of school-age children competing with each other in a violent, futuristic war game. However, Red Rising takes many of the concepts from Hunger Games and makes them more INTENSE. While it has its drawbacks, the book was more than good enough to make me hunger for volume 2. Golden Son exceeded Red Rising, in my mind, in virtually every conceivable way. More action, more character growth, and a stunning final scene that is one of the most cruel cliffhangers I have ever encountered. This is NOT a typical slow-moving, filler novel to get you from book one to book three of the trilogy. Instead of slowing things down, Pierce Brown pumped the gas at the start of Golden Son and never let up. Now we arrive at Morning Star. I can't tell yet where I would place it in the hierarchy of the three books; my enjoyment of it and the anticipation built from the other two installments are too tightly intertwined. I will say this: it is a worthy conclusion that thankfully does not reach for a pie in the sky perfect ending. We all realize that those don't exist in real life, and many of us don't care to have it happen in our literature, either. Darrow and his friends, as usual, encounter a great deal of adversity and triumph throughout. I love how they bicker, how they stick together, how they take chances, how some of them don't make it to the end. There are unrealistic moments in the book; a couple of them made me cringe. But the fact remains that Pierce Brown has woven an intricate tapestry of people and ideas that already have me thinking about reading it again. And again. People, if you haven't started reading this trilogy yet, I urge you to do so. The world Mr. Brown built is all too recognizable, because humanity embodies the very best and worst of all of the Society's Colors. You can enjoy these books on a macro level with its societal commentary, or on a micro level, with its burgeoning relationships and the minutiae of living and dying. But bloodydamn enjoy these books.

I was very pleased with this version of Cremo Cologne for Men (Spice & Black Vanilla). Although palates and senses of smell can vary greatly, this is an outstanding choice for some basic reasons. This is definitely a warm, Oriental-inspired fragrance labeled for men, but it could arguably be labeled as unisex as well. I have roughly one hundred or so different men's fragrances and cologne oils for reference. For those who've been around the block with men's fragrances, this will likely conjure up a middling similarity to Viktor & Rolf's Spicebomb and Versace's Eros. Spice & Black Vanilla also shares some space with Jean Paul Gaultier's Le Male Elixir. All are excellent choices in their own way, but seem related, sort of like first or second cousins. Spice & Black Vanilla falls on that spectrum between Spicebomb and Le Male Elixir, edging closer to Spicebomb. If anyone might have thought the Black Vanilla in this formulation is close to Mancera's Black Vanilla, think again. Mancera's interpretation of Black Vanilla contains more of a controlled fire that makes a clear play for dominance, whereas Spice & Black Vanilla plays a more reserved game but is more than capable of a swift checkmate. Cremo's concoction also seems to flirt by employing a hint of neroli (bitter orange), but if so, blends it so well that it never goes past the flirtation stage. As a final recommendation, this is most certainly a cool/cold weather fragrance for autumn and winter. It also inspires romance or closeness so restrict its wear to late evening and nighttime activities. Sillage (projection) on this item is quite good so you can reasonably expect 4-6 hours of play, depending on your activity and body chemistry. Don't be surprised though if it "sticks" to you or your clothing though. Some of the very best do just that, and mellow into something even better as the day or night moves on. There are many more colognes that cost hundreds more and would have a hard time competing to keep up with this one. This was a blind buy for me as I've used Cremo body wash products for men and wanted to try their hand in the cologne space. I do not regret this purchase in the least and I'll definitely see what else Cremo has to offer in men's colognes.

Timely delivery, product was as pictured, (hardcover). I stopped recreational reading for over half a decade. This is the second book I've read cover-to-cover since having started reading for fun again 2 months ago. I'm not sure whether it's because I haven't read in awhile or because Stephen King is a great writer, (or both) but this book is stellar. *Spoilers ahead* The prologue of this book is a continuation of the epilogue, interestingly. I highly recommend revisiting the prologue after finishing the book. As Stephen King novels often do, things end on a sad note. For the most part, however, the plot is wrapped up nice and tidy, (with the exception of Father Callahan- I think that King did this on purpose. It's not horror if there isn't anything to leave the reader scared of after finishing a story). It is heavily implied that the Ben and Mark return to Jerusalem's Lot to deal with the remaining vampire thralls that Barlow left. King really makes an effort to develop the character of so many of the town's citizens, and this makes the sense of loss more gripping than most horror novels. At the end, I was left feeling a desire for more closure- I wanted to read about Ben and Mark clearing the town house-by-house after returning to it. I wanted to know what ended up happening to Father Callahan. But again, it's a horror novel- a Stephen King horror novel at that. I consider it lucky that the subplots that were tied up nicely were tied up at all.
